section.title: Reward–safety conflict
section.learnings: In a constrained task, earning more reward usually means incurring more cost. Benchmark authors build their tasks this way on purpose. CRAX says so of all its tasks: "achieving high reward typically requires incurring higher cost" (Tomilin 2026 §1). Safety-Gymnasium says it of its velocity tasks: "agents aim for higher reward by moving faster, but they must also adhere to velocity constraints" (Ji 2023 §4.1). In these benchmarks the conflict exists in every context, so by itself it does not make one context harder than another. What matters for a curriculum is where in Ω the costly shortcut lies, because a curriculum that looks only at reward will move there. Koprulu 2025 §4.2 shows this happening: CURROT moved its goals straight through the hazards.

section.title: Over-conservatism
section.learnings: A constrained agent can learn to satisfy the constraint and fail to reach high reward. In CRAX, PPO-Lag is the only method that satisfies every bound on Levels 2 and 3, and it "fails to reach high rewards" (Tomilin 2026 §5.1). On Pathway and Height, training directly on Level 3 "yields overly conservative policies that underutilize the available safety budget" (§5.2). These are the two suites where the CRAX level curriculum helped.

section.title: Violation-dominated exploration
section.learnings: A constrained agent can keep violating the constraint while it explores and make little progress. CRAX says this of direct training on Level 3 in general: "exploration becomes dominated by constraint violations and sparse progress" (Tomilin 2026 §5.2). On Goal, the suite I use, PPO-Lag reaches reward 7.0 on Level 3 against 34.8 on Level 1 (Table 5). Goal is the suite where the CRAX level curriculum did not help.

section.title: Constraint generalisation
section.learnings: A policy that is safe on the contexts it trained on is often unsafe on contexts it has not seen. Four groups report this with five different kinds of shift: patient physiology (Kwon 2026: "policies satisfying constraints during training frequently violate safety requirements on unseen patients"), gravity, mass and friction (Kwon 2025), sim-to-real (As 2025), perturbed dynamics (Queeney 2023), and unseen procedural levels (Kenton 2019, counting catastrophes rather than a cost constraint). Training on q and deploying on w is such a shift.

section.title: λ at a distribution change
section.learnings: Three facts about the Lagrange multiplier λ. Under a fixed distribution it oscillates around the cost limit and overshoots (Stooke 2020 §1: "we witnessed numerous problematic cases", with a 90° phase lag between λ and cost). The value it needs changes with the task and with the cost limit (Spoor 2025). After a distribution change it can be far off (Chen 2024, "Lagrangian mismatch" between a multiplier learned offline and the one online training needs; the reported values are about 1500 versus 0.65). A curriculum is a sequence of distribution changes. I found no paper that measures λ across one. My velocity-ant collapse (λ 1.5 → 405 at the level switch) is a first observation.
section.annotation: The 1500 / 0.65 figures come from Chen 2024 §3.2 as extracted by the deep-research run; the abstract confirms the phenomenon, the numbers themselves I have not opened. Check before citing them.

page.learnings: SCG, the safe curriculum of Koprulu 2025, only proposes contexts where the current policy's cost is already under a threshold (eq. 4). This targets violation-dominated exploration. It does not target over-conservatism, because a safe policy with low reward passes the filter. We should expect SCG to help in one of these two and not in the other.
page.contribution:
TeachMyAgent evaluates curriculum methods by building one task distribution per property that makes teaching hard (mostly infeasible, mostly trivial, ...) and running every method on each. I do the same for constrained RL. Each property above becomes one distribution over Ω that isolates it, and the question per distribution is which curriculum methods still train a policy that is safe and performant on w:
(1) where in Ω the reward–safety conflict sits
(2) over-conservatism on w
(3) violation-dominated exploration on w
(4) constraint generalisation from q to w
(5) λ at a curriculum switch For property 5 I found no measurement and already have one observation. My earlier properties 2 (few contexts feasible) and 3 (rare hard tail) are replaced by the two failures that CRAX reports.
